claims.text: Experimental models and observational studies suggest that vitamin E supplementation may prevent cardiovascular disease and cancer.
Nine of 11 trials testing high-dosage vitamin E (>=400 IU/d) showed increased risk for all-cause mortality in comparisons of vitamin E versus control.
The pooled all-cause mortality risk difference in high-dosage vitamin E trials was 39 per 10,000 persons (95% CI, 3 to 74 per 10,000 persons; P = 0.035).
In low-dosage vitamin E trials, the all-cause mortality risk difference was -16 per 10,000 persons (95% CI, -41 to 10 per 10,000 persons; P > 0.2).
Dose-response analysis demonstrates a statistically significant relationship between vitamin E dosage and all-cause mortality, with increased risk at dosages greater than 150 IU/d.
High-dosage (>=400 IU/d) vitamin E supplements may increase all-cause mortality.

evidence.description: Experimental models and observational studies suggest that vitamin E supplementation may prevent cardiovascular disease and cancer.
9 of 11 trials testing high-dosage vitamin E (> or =400 IU/d) showed increased risk (risk difference > 0) for all-cause mortality in comparisons of vitamin E versus control.
The pooled all-cause mortality risk difference in high-dosage vitamin E trials was 39 per 10,000 persons (95% CI, 3 to 74 per 10,000 persons; P = 0.035).
For low-dosage vitamin E trials, the risk difference was -16 per 10,000 persons (CI, -41 to 10 per 10,000 persons; P > 0.2).
A dose-response analysis showed a statistically significant relationship between vitamin E dosage and all-cause mortality, with increased risk of dosages greater than 150 IU/d.
The pooled all-cause mortality risk difference in high-dosage vitamin E trials was 39 per 10,000 persons (95% CI, 3 to 74 per 10,000 persons; P = 0.035).

methodologies.name: Dose-response meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
methodologies.description: A meta-analysis synthesizing data across 19 randomized controlled trials to evaluate the dose-response relationship between vitamin E supplementation and all-cause mortality.
conditions: Vitamin E combined with other vitamins or minerals (10 trials)
Vitamin E dosage ranging from 16.5 to 2000 IU/d (median 400 IU/d)

limitations.text: High-dosage (>=400 IU/d) trials were often small and were performed in patients with chronic diseases.
The generalizability of the findings to healthy adults is uncertain.
Precise estimation of the threshold at which risk increases is difficult.
